item.title: The question of the closed border
item.description: The question of the closed border
item.content:encoded:
Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin

Preemptive efforts to contain the New World screwworm outbreak have led to painful trade-offs — including the closure of the southern border to livestock imports for over a year. | Fernando Llano/AP
QUICK FIX

— State ag officials and Republican lawmakers are debating whether to reopen the southern border to livestock amid the New World screwworm outbreak.

— MA sat down with a nutrition leader to discuss changes to federal food aid and an anticipated school meals rule.

— The Department of Agriculture has expanded grazing access on public lands as part of an effort to rebuild the domestic herd.

IT’S MONDAY, JUNE 15. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send tips and pitches to rshin@politico.com, reach me securely on Signal at rshin.80 and follow us at @Morning_Ag for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
DRIVING THE DAY

ON THE BORDERLINE: Preemptive efforts to contain the New World screwworm outbreak have led to painful trade-offs — including the closure of the southern border to livestock imports for over a year.

The border will stay closed indefinitely, Ag Secretary Brooke Rollins said Thursday.

But the question of opening the border to livestock is quietly looming as screwworm dominates the industry’s attention, and some Republicans and state officials say reopening the border must not fall out of sight.

“We continue to have those discussions with USDA about properly reopening the border sooner rather than later,” New Mexico Agriculture Secretary Jeff Witte told MA.

“They understand the need and the impacts on commerce in both directions. There's some things that have to be settled in Mexico, and reassurances have to be made,” he added. “But everybody's on the same page that, in fact, the border does need to open.”

Some Republican lawmakers voiced similar stances: Reopening the U.S.-Mexico border to livestock imports remains high on their to-do list — with proper precautions.

“Probably what we could do to help bring down the cost of hamburger, though, is to open up our borders,” Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) said, adding that “the horse is out of the barn here” already with screwworm.

Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.) said he supports opening parts of the border, specifically the western side, which is cooler and has “had zero screwworm problems.”

House Ag Chair G.T. Thompson (R-Pa.) said during a hearing with Rollins on June 4 that it is important to “have frank conversations about returning to a sense of normalcy at the border.” The closure has halted cattle imports from Mexico, leading it to build out its own meat processing infrastructure independent of the United States, Thompson said.

“We need to keep talking about next best steps for the southern border, including a reopening that includes rigorous checkpoints, treatment and quarantine measures,” Thompson said at the hearing.

Thompson later told MA that there are “probably at least a million head of cattle on the Mexican side that normally would be in the United States and in those feed lots in Texas.”

But, but, but: Rollins told reporters livestock restrictions on the southern border will remain firmly in place for the time being.

“We've had the ports closed for a year now, so we have not let any animals across the [southern] ports because it is so close to Texas, but we haven't let them in through New Mexico or Arizona either,” Rollins said. “That will obviously continue until we have a better understanding of what we're dealing with.”

Some Republicans said ramping livestock imports back up amid the parasite’s threat will only cause more pain.

Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) said easing restrictions on the border could increase the probability of further screwworm incursions, noting, “That consequence is deadly and will damage the supply of beef.” Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) expressed similar concern, saying Mexican cattle imports carry the threat of diminishing the U.S. herd.

USDA had confirmed 12 cases of screwworm in the U.S. as of Sunday night.

A spokesperson for the department told MA in a statement that “first and foremost, USDA is focused on containment and eventual eradication of NWS,” but the department is evaluating every day “the possibility of re-opening ports.”
 

Watch Gavin Newsom on On the Road with Jonathan Martin

Gov. Gavin Newsom joins Jonathan Martin in San Francisco for a candid conversation on the experiences that shaped his political career, his approach to Trump and what he sees at stake for Democrats in 2026.
Watch the interview.

 
 
NUTRITION PROGRAMS

MA Q&A: Federal food policy is reshaping the market for fruit and vegetable growers on multiple fronts. The Trump administration has reorganized the Food and Nutrition Administration, the USDA agency formerly called the Food and Nutrition Service that administers school meal programs, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children — programs that represent a major outlet for the produce industry.

A new school meal rule expected to be released later this summer could revise nutrition standards to align more closely with the new Dietary Guidelines for Americans.

Mollie Van Lieu, vice president of nutrition and health policy at the International Fresh Produce Association, spoke with MA about how her organization is navigating the changes.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What is IFPA’s stance on the recent reorganization of the Food and Nutrition Administration?

We're definitely watching that closely. Certainly the programs that FNS administers, particularly school meals and WIC, are really significant markets for the fruit and vegetable industry and American fruit and vegetable growers. So we're working with and speaking with child nutrition directors to make sure that they will continue to get the resources they need.

We definitely work with career staff, and we don't want to see research that's done on these programs reduced.

How is IPFA translating the Dietary Guidelines for Americans into its lobbying strategy on Capitol Hill?

The new dietary guidelines are pretty consistent with previous dietary guidelines as it relates to fruits and vegetables and serving amounts.

School meals definitely [are] impacted the most because you have to serve from all five vegetable subgroups. So that's something we're watching because in the new dietary guidelines, they didn't explicitly mention the five vegetable subgroups.

So with the administration announcing that they'll be putting out a new school meal rule, probably later this summer, we’ll see if that will impact the nutrition standards that require schools to serve vegetables from all five of those subgroups.

We're definitely talking to the Hill about that and what that has meant for us growers and just diversity of vegetables that kids are having access to.

What is IFPA’s stance on the new SNAP stocking standards rule?

Most traditional grocers, where 90 percent of people are redeeming SNAP benefits, easily meet the new stocking standards.

In the smaller [stores] where there are barriers, we also have to make sure that we're spurring demand, too, because people can't eat something that they don't have access to. We're willing to work with those retailers that might be having challenges.

AROUND THE AGENCIES

OPEN RANGE: USDA directed U.S. Forest Service employees to expand grazing access on National Forest System lands, advising field offices to reopen vacant and closed allotments and streamline permitting to increase grazing capacity.

The order advances a March memorandum of understanding between Rollins and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to boost the domestic cattle herd.

Rollins framed the move as a rebuke of regulatory creep.

“For too long, bureaucratic overreach and activist-driven lawfare have undermined the multiple-use mandate of our National Forests and Grasslands,” Rollins in a statement on the directive.

The directive also called for better coordination with permittees during wildfires and more flexibility on drought relief grazing.
Row Crops

— The Food and Drug Administration issued an emergency use authorization for a generic over-the-counter treatment for screwworm infestation in pets.

— Inside the Department of Health and Human Services, workers say the dysfunction of the DOGE era persists, our Sophie Gardner reports.

— JBS, the world’s largest meatpacker, is preparing to close a beef-processing plant in Pennsylvania, the latest facility to close as a cattle shortage in the U.S. squeezes meatpacking companies. (The Wall Street Journal)

— The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention announced a multistate outbreak of infant botulism linked to the recalled Nara Organics Whole Milk Organic Infant Formula.

item.title: Republicans push USMCA renewal
item.content:encoded:
Presented by U.S. Farmers & Ranchers in Action: Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin

Presented by U.S. Farmers & Ranchers in Action

With help from Grace Yarrow and Marcia Brown

President Donald Trump told reporters on June 10 that he may terminate USMCA because “we don't need anything that Canada has, we don’t need anything that Mexico has.” | Getty Images
QUICK FIX

— Ag Republicans are urging the White House to renew the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, in light of President Donald Trump’s indication that he would not.

— The Senate farm bill text is poised to drop tomorrow.

— Maine had a plan to feed its hungry. Then came Trump's “big beautiful bill.”

IT’S MONDAY, JUNE 22. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send tips and pitches to rshin@politico.com, get in touch securely on Signal at rshin.80 and follow us at @Morning_Ag for more.
 

A message from U.S. Farmers & Ranchers in Action:

A new S&P Global Energy analysis, commissioned by U.S. Farmers and Ranchers in Action, explores how expanded biofuel markets could help create new demand for agriculture, strengthen energy and food security, and power long-term growth. Discover what the future could look like by 2050. Read the report.
 

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
DRIVING THE DAY

TRADE TROUBLES: Farm-state Republicans are urging Trump to reconsider his stance on USMCA after he suggested he would abandon the trade deal weeks ahead of its July mandatory review.

Senate Ag Chair John Boozman (R-Ark.) told your host that he has spoken with the White House and is “encouraging that we get a new commitment signed as soon as possible.”

“USMCA is very important, and I think that the president will ultimately negotiate a good deal,” Boozman said. “It was one of his centerpiece achievements of his last administration.”

Trump told reporters on June 10 that he was erring on the side of terminating the trade agreement because “we don't need anything that Canada has, we don’t need anything that Mexico has.”

The Trump administration is conducting formal negotiations with Mexico and recently opened discussions with Canada as part of the six-year review of USMCA. Under the deal’s “sunset review” provision, all three countries must meet on July 1 to say whether they want to renew the pact for another 16 years.

Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) told MA that she hopes “the White House is going to reconsider” letting the deal expire because USMCA is “a wonderful trade agreement for our ag producers.” Other senators similarly emphasized the deal has been a boon to American farmers and the broader economies of the participating nations.

“It's pretty clear to me, and I hope everybody else, even the president of the United States, that … it's beneficial to all three countries,” Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) told reporters last week.

Republicans are holding out hope that despite Trump’s suggestions that he will not renew USMCA, he will change his mind come July. Sen. John Hoeven (R-N.D.) said his negative comments about the pact may have just been “Art of the Deal”-style gamesmanship.

“The president likes to keep the other party off balance in any negotiation,” Hoeven said. “I think that may be his negotiating style so that they don’t assume we’re going to get it just the way it is.”

Key context: If one or more countries object to renewing USMCA, the agreement would expire in 2036, unless negotiators resolve outstanding concerns in annual reviews over the next 10 years.

Any of the countries could terminate the agreement with six months’ notice, though both Mexico and Canada have sent letters to the Trump administration saying they support renewing the deal.
 

A message from U.S. Farmers & Ranchers in Action:
 
On the Hill

FARM BILL INCOMING: Boozman is set to release his farm bill text tomorrow, according to three people familiar with the conversations, Grace reports. The bill will tee up a fight over Democrats’ nutrition demands and some Republican priorities that aren’t expected to be included.

Committee staff will privately brief Senate Agriculture Committee members and industry groups today ahead of the bill's introduction, according to the people, who were granted anonymity to discuss the private plans.

Boozman’s plan is expected to omit some controversial GOP priorities in an effort to secure enough Democratic support to clear the Senate’s 60-vote threshold.

Boozman said he is aiming to mark up the bill between the chamber's Fourth of July and August recesses.

The sticking point: Democrats have said they will not support a farm bill package that doesn’t delay the implementation of a provision included in the GOP’s domestic policy package that will soon force some states to foot part of the bill for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits. It’s not clear whether Boozman’s base text will include the SNAP cost-share delay.

“I don't know that the chairman has made a decision on if it has to be a partisan markup,” said one ag lobbyist familiar with the talks, also granted anonymity to discuss them.

Republicans’ megalaw already granted a group of states with the highest SNAP error rates an implementation delay to give them more time to reduce inaccurate payments. States with error rates under 6 percent won’t have to foot the bill at all.

“The real challenge is the fact that Republicans have already made an exception,” the lobbyist noted. “If there was no exception, I think they would have an easier time holding the line, but the political dynamics are just tough.”
 

J.B. Pritzker talks Democrats’ road ahead

On On the Road, Jonathan Martin sits down with Gov. J.B. Pritzker at Manny’s Deli for a candid conversation on 2028 speculation, party strategy and the future of Democratic politics.
Watch now.

 
 
SNAP CHATS

THE FOOD SECURITY OUTLOOK: Last year’s passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act has set in motion one of the biggest transformations of the welfare state that the U.S. has seen in decades.

For more than a generation, SNAP — which provides roughly 40 million people with money for groceries — has served as the country’s dominant vector for direct payments to people struggling to eat. But SNAP’s era as arguably the nation’s preeminent anti-poverty program may be ending.

Already 3.5 million people nationwide have been booted from the program, and as the law’s new eligibility terms take effect this year, more are likely to follow, while others will be abruptly sent back into a workforce for which they are unprepared. Roughly 45,000 people in Maine, including veterans and homeless adults — briefly granted a reprieve from work requirements during the Biden administration — will be newly required to work or volunteer.

In few places has the response been as swift as in Maine, where Democratic Gov. Janet Mills, legislative leaders and state nonprofits seven years ago committed to a 2030 goal of ensuring Mainers always have enough to eat. Now that ambitious objective — one that officials and activists believed was within reach for a small state with a motivated government, even after pandemic-era setbacks — seems even further away.

Instead, lawmakers, nonprofits and bureaucrats now see themselves spending the remainder of the decade trying to manage the impact of a federal law that will make it harder for millions of people to obtain federal nutrition assistance and health care while passing significant costs onto states.

“What makes it difficult is knowing it’s not sustainable,” said Maine Speaker of the House Ryan Fecteau at the state house, bleary-eyed in a worn long-sleeve tee and vest after presiding over several days of late-night sessions in April to deliver the budget and other priorities.

Read Marcia’s full magazine piece here.

Navigate policy challenges with confidence. POLITICO Pro gives professionals authoritative reporting, expert analysis and powerful tools to understand the business of government — in Washington and beyond. Learn more about POLITICO Pro.

 
 
Row Crops

— The Senate Appropriations committee will mark up the ag-FDA budget for fiscal 2027 on Thursday.

— Three more New World screwworm cases were detected over the weekend, bringing the total count to 15 as of Sunday evening.

— Zach Lahn, a businessman and farmer who beat a Trump-backed candidate for Iowa’s Republican nomination for governor, is selling himself as a political outsider eager to bust up big agriculture interests. (The Wall Street Journal)

— Over 60 farm, food and health groups filed a petition urging the Food and Drug Administration to end routine use of medically important antibiotics for disease prevention in livestock production.

item.title: TPS decision could reshape ag labor market
item.description: TPS decision could reshape ag labor market
item.content:encoded:
Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Marcia Brown

With help from Ellie Borst
QUICK FIX

— The Supreme Court ruling allowing the Trump administration to end temporary protected status for more than 1 million immigrants could make it harder for meatpackers and others in the food supply chain to hire enough workers.

— The Make America Healthy Again movement isn’t satisfied by President Donald Trump’s executive order promoting regenerative agriculture.

— Confirmed New World screwworm cases in the United States are ticking up.  

IT’S MONDAY, JUNE 29. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Marcia Brown. Send tips to marciabrown@politico.com and get in touch securely on Signal at marciagbrown.68. Don’t forget to follow us at @Morning_Ag for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
DRIVING THE DAY

TEMPORARY PROTECTED STATUS: A Supreme Court ruling last week that will make it easier for the Trump administration to deport certain immigrants could also add new labor market pressures in the food supply chains, analysts say.

The decision could pave the way for Trump to end temporary protected status for people from Syria and Haiti and also make it easier for Trump to end TPS for people from countries facing war, natural disasters or other challenges. The ruling could upend the lives of roughly a million people and may make it harder for meatpackers and other employers to find enough people to work.

Nearly a third of meatpacking workers in the U.S. are foreign-born, according to the Migration Policy Institute, and many of those hold temporary protected status, an immigration designation that allows people to live and work legally in the U.S.

“The effects of this ruling will be felt by more than just those directly impacted — every worker, every community and the entire economy will feel it,” said Milton Jones, president of the United Food and Commercial Workers International Union. “It jeopardizes worker and food safety in meatpacking plants, food processing facilities and grocery stores, with workers left behind being pushed to their limit without the skilled hands of their immigrant co-workers next to them.”

With the court’s blessing, the Trump administration can begin deportation proceedings against Syrians and Haitians, if they cannot obtain another legal status, such as asylum or work visas. Other TPS recipients from countries like Venezuela and Afghanistan are also expected to be affected by the court’s ruling. Many have lived in the U.S. for decades and have children who are U.S. citizens.

Terminating TPS, combined with ending other refugee and humanitarian programs, could result in a 20 percent cut in jobs at poultry plants in the Delmarva Peninsula, according to a warning from Mountaire Farms’ executive Zach Evans obtained by Civil Eats this year.

“The Supreme Court ruling is likely to further stress the labor supply at meatpacking plants across the country,” Alejandro Gutierrez-Li, an immigration economist at North Carolina State University, told MA, noting that meatpackers can’t easily access the H-2A visa program for year-round work like meatpacking. “Research has shown that, even in periods of high unemployment, Americans prefer to pass on physically demanding jobs at meatpacking plants.”

“If you look at the history of the industry, it’s basically been built on immigrant labor for a century, going back to the late 1800s,” said Derrell Peel, an agricultural economist at Oklahoma State University focused on the beef industry.

The meatpacking industry downplayed the impact of the TPS ruling. 

“Our members have largely transitioned away from this workforce,” said Sarah Little, a spokesperson for the Meat Institute, a trade group that represents large meatpacking companies. “The ruling will not have much impact on the industry as a whole at this stage.”

Still, the Supreme Court ruling comes at a time when beef meatpackers are paying record prices for cattle and losing money. Meatpackers have already raised wages and benefits since the coronavirus pandemic as they aim to recruit more workers to jobs that are difficult and dangerous.

What’s next: It's not clear how quickly the administration will act, but UFCW is urging the administration to give TPS recipients more time to plan “before forcing them to leave their homes.”

Gutierrez-Li noted the labor market pressures could eventually be passed on to consumers in the form of higher consumer prices and lead the U.S. to increase beef imports.

“Plants that are not capable of replacing their TPS workers may decide to close,” he told MA. “In rural areas with few employers, this could have broader negative impacts on the local economy.”

Michelle Mittelstadt, a spokesperson for the Migration Policy Institute, said “only Congress” can act to create more permanent immigration protections for Haitian and Syrian TPS recipients, but it would need three-fifths of the Senate as required by the Immigration Act of 1990, “which seems quite unlikely in the current political environment.”
At the White House

Trump signed an order late Thursday aimed at reducing farm chemical use on food crops, a gesture toward a disillusioned MAHA coalition, Ellie Borst of POLITICO’s E&E News reports.

The executive order establishes advancing "private-sector innovation in farm modernization" and other regenerative agriculture practices as U.S. policy. But it stops short of many regulatory changes pushed by MAHA advocates, who are challenging Trump's allegiance to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s mission to reduce risky chemical exposures.

"This EO does nothing for chemical regulation but kick the can down the road," said Vani Hari, a MAHA influencer and food blogger with a close relationship to Kennedy, in a post on X.

The executive order came the same day the Supreme Court sided with Bayer, which makes Roundup, in a decision that makes it harder for people to sue the company. Bayer has been facing billions of dollars in liability from lawsuits alleging Roundup, the brand name for glyphosate, causes cancer.

The White House had sided with industry in an amicus brief, as Pamela King and your host reported, sparking MAHA’s ire. But the court’s decision made a preplanned dinner last week at the White House for regenerative farmers a bit … awkward.

Guests’ party favors? Organic seed packets.

The Trump administration has sought to balance the priorities of a longtime GOP constituency, farmers, while pleasing the president’s relatively new allies in the MAHA movement. The same day of the executive order, USDA also announced a new regulation that would allow regenerative farmers to access premium prices in biofuels markets.

Trade groups celebrated the new rule.

“This new rule is an important step forward, and we believe it will help jumpstart opportunities for growers who are committed to doing what’s right for the land and the environment, while being recognized for their efforts,” Mark Mueller, an Iowa farmer and president of the Iowa Corn Growers Association, said in a statement.

SPEAKING OF MAHA: Our Jessie Blaeser has an illuminating new analysis of what The POLITICO Poll revealed about the MAHA movement. Even MAHA supporters are divided over reducing vaccines, she noted, and while many MAHA principles have support across the political spectrum, the issue of reducing vaccines shows the biggest partisan split.

On the other hand, there’s broad support for a lot of MAHA principles, including eating more healthy food and reducing exposure to harmful chemicals, even among people who don’t identify as part of MAHA.
AROUND THE AGENCIES

THE NEXT TURN OF THE SCREW(WORM): At least 27 cases of the New World screwworm have been detected in New Mexico and Texas, with new cases popping up over the last week, according to the latest numbers from USDA.

The larvae have been found in cattle, sheep, goats and one dog. The pest can be deadly for livestock, and monitoring, treatment and prevention are costly for ranchers.

While the New World screwworm was regularly found in the U.S. in the 1960s, the production of sterile male flies, which drive down the population by mating with female flies, previously eradicated the pest from the U.S.

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins joined Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on Saturday for the opening of a new facility in Chiapas, Mexico, designed to contain the spread of the flesh-eating pest. The facility will produce 100 million sterile flies weekly by the fall, but former USDA officials have said the Trump administration’s internal federal spending reviews delayed its opening — and that it could have been open as early as this spring, as your host previously reported.

The new facility will double the current capacity for sterile fly production, but experts have said it’s still not enough to push the fly out of the U.S.

USDA demurred when asked about a timeline for U.S. eradication. Dudley Hoskins, the department’s undersecretary for marketing and regulatory programs, recently told the Texas House Agriculture and Livestock Committee that 500 million sterile flies are needed to drive out the pest.

A third USDA facility in Texas intended to produce more sterile flies is not yet online.

According to USDA, Rollins may hold another screwworm press briefing, “likely this week.”

FIRST IN MA: Anti-monopoly and progressive groups including the American Economic Liberties Project and Demand Progress are sending a letter to Senate Ag Committee leaders today urging them to oppose including any version of the Save Our Bacon Act, language that would preempt state animal welfare laws like California’s Proposition 12, in the farm bill. The Senate farm bill does not include the language, but the House version does.
Row Crops

— Reps. G.T. Thompson (R-Pa.) and Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Mich.) introduced the Local Foods for Healthy Schools Act, which would reinstate a program that the Trump administration canceled last year.

— The DOJ sued four states led by Democratic governors, demanding they turn over the sensitive data of food aid applicants to USDA, your host reported.

— USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service issued a public health alert for ready-to-eat chicken Caesar wrap products for potential listeria contamination. USDA didn’t request a recall because the products are no longer for sale.

— Rollins sent a letter to New York Gov. Kathy Hochul asking about the “rapid expansion of large-scale solar development on New York farmland.”

item.title: USMCA’s clouded ag future
item.content:encoded:
Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin

With help from Grace Yarrow

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said the agricultural trade deficit was a factor in the administration's decision not to renew USMCA. | Mark Schiefelbein/AP
QUICK FIX

— Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said ag trade deficits influenced President Donald Trump's decision not to renew the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement.

— Labor unions and nonprofits moved to halt the Agriculture Department’s reorganization, arguing department officials acknowledged their proposals will lead to mass resignations.

— Rollins signed a memorandum of understanding seeking to combat lawfare against farmers related to use of their land.

IT’S MONDAY, JULY 6. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send tips to rshin@politico.com and get in touch securely on Signal at rshin.80. Follow your favorite ag team at @Morning_Ag for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
DRIVING THE DAY

TRADE TALKS: Rollins said agricultural trade deficits with Mexico and Canada were factors in Trump’s decision not to renew USMCA but that the deal’s future isn’t so bleak.

“The president believes that there are some inefficiencies in the current system, that we have a pretty big trade deficit with both of those countries and especially in agriculture, and that he is working to solve for that,” Rollins told MA when asked about USMCA at a news conference Thursday. “Now, it doesn't mean that the agreement just goes by the wayside.”

Rollins told MA that Trump is moving toward a new agreement or “multiples of agreements” with Mexico and Canada that are more advantageous for American producers. She added that the president is “very involved in every detail of all of these decisions.”

Ag trade leaders had mixed reactions to the abstention to renew and the renegotiation process. Some said it risks sluggishness, while others cheered it as a way to win industry-friendly updates.

“There's a negotiating round set up with Mexico, so I think there is really an attempt there to work out some technical details,” said an ag industry leader familiar with the administration’s strategy, granted anonymity to speak candidly. “But because there's really no signs of progress with Canada, I think realistically the kind of protracted ongoing negotiation is likely.”

The person added that the exit of Daniel Watson, who served as the assistant U.S. trade representative for the Western Hemisphere until the end of June, could further hamper progress.

“It is interesting that the USTR lead is retiring,” the ag industry representative said. “That's going to slow things down, I think.”

Watson said he would return to “the trade table” in the coming months.

The ag industry representative said the biggest agricultural sticking point in the deal is seasonality provisions with Mexico, which is “the only one that might actually change the terms of the agreement.”

Seasonal American produce growers, concentrated in Florida and Georgia, argue that Mexican fresh produce floods the U.S. market during their harvest windows, undercutting prices when domestic supply is highest, and that the trade framework doesn’t go far enough to protect U.S. growers.

Mike Joyner, president of the Florida Fruit and Vegetable Association, said he supports the administration’s move not to renew USMCA because it provides more time to work in stricter seasonality provisions.

“I would rather them take their time, address our issue and all the other issues they need to address, and then sign a deal that works for everybody because right now, USMCA doesn't work for our members,” Joyner told MA.

“I'm encouraged that they're not going to sign a deal until they get a good deal, because we just have to have changes in this update,” he added.

Key context: USMCA remains in place for the next decade with annual reviews until the three sides can agree on renewal or it expires in 2036.

The U.S. and Mexico plan to meet July 20 for a third round of negotiations, and the U.S. and Canada are continuing talks.
AROUND THE AGENCIES

STOP RIGHT THERE: A coalition of unions and other groups is renewing efforts to halt USDA's reorganization, citing previously undisclosed documents showing the department expects nearly a quarter of its employees to quit rather than relocate, as our Hassan Ali Kanu and Grace report.

The reduction-in-force plan documents, which were previously confidential, were submitted to a federal judge in California late Wednesday as part of a continuing bid to halt or reverse the Trump administration’s campaign to cut the size of the federal government.

The reorganization was intended to reduce USDA's workforce “by approximately 23,177 which is a 23% overall reduction,” according to the 2025 internal planning documents. Officials added that they expect that “a significant number of employees will decline geographic reassignments.”

Thousands of USDA employees across the country took buyout offers last year, and unions have warned that most employees who declined buyout offers would also decline offers to relocate.

Approximately 2,600 Washington-area positions are set to relocate to “regional hubs” across the country during the reorganization. USDA expects relocated employees to move this summer, Deputy Agriculture Secretary Stephen Vaden said earlier this year.

“All aspects of” relocation must be completed within one year of the effective reassignment date, according to answers on a list of FAQs about the reassignment plan obtained by POLITICO last month. Employees who decline to relocate will effectively resign or retire, according to the department.

USDA leaders also said they would be reviewing the number of employees who opted to take buyouts to see “if any further downsizing is needed” in “the coming weeks.”

The unions filed new motions Wednesday to halt the sweeping reorganization of USDA, arguing the plans are aimed at gutting the workforce rather than efficiency.
IN THE COURTS

IN THE NAME OF THE LAW: Rollins and Small Business Administrator Kelly Loeffler signed a memorandum of understanding Thursday to oppose government overreach they say has been weaponized against farmers. They said the MOU formalizes the collaboration of their agencies on the issue.

Rollins and Loeffler said regulations created in the interest of environmental groups have resulted in fines and the seizure of farmland from producers.

“Families who have worked the land for generations — fourth, fifth, sixth, eighth, 10th generations — have fallen victim to all kinds of reckless environmental lawfare,” Rollins said at a press conference Thursday. “These attacks on American farm- and ranchland represent an existential threat to everything we hold dear in this country.”

Rollins said USDA will continue to investigate lawfare claims reported through its lawfare portal. She said the portal has received over 600 submissions since its launch in April of last year.

“We work through this portal meticulously and daily, we have very late-night Zoom calls to talk all of the cases through,” she said.
Row Crops

Presented by Bayer

With help from Jacob Wendler

Congress's August recess is looming as lawmakers return to Washington today. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
QUICK FIX

— Ag Republicans are staring down a tall legislative to-do list and growing obstacles before they leave for the August recess.

— Ag Secretary Brooke Rollins is scheduled to attend an event tonight celebrating 250 years of American agriculture, which attendees could pay up to $15,000 to sponsor, according to event materials.

— A new poll found record-high voter support for year-round E15 sales legislation.

IT’S MONDAY, JULY 13. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send story tips to rshin@politico.com and get in touch securely on Signal at rshin.80. Follow your favorite ag team at @Morning_Ag for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
 

A message from Bayer:

At Bayer, we empower American farms with the smarter tools needed to advance regenerative agriculture. By providing accurate, real-time data maps, we give farmers necessary insights to improve soil health and protect the land for generations. When farmers are equipped to care for their soil with tools like real-data maps, stronger yields and a sustainable bottom line naturally follow. Learn more.
 
DRIVING THE DAY

SO MANY BILLS, SO LITTLE TIME: August recess is fast approaching, and with it, mounting urgency for Congress to advance a slew of ag legislation.

The Senate farm bill awaits a markup, and President Donald Trump has requested over $11 billion in farm assistance in a supplemental package with military funding.

Then there’s the perennial push for year-round nationwide E15 sales and other nagging question marks, like the effort to undo hemp sale restrictions, set to take effect in November. The weeks between now and August will be about triaging.

“I wish we could get a farm bill before the election, but I think that's going to come after the election,” Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) told reporters last week. “E15 is very critical to farmers voting in the midterm elections, and so I would expect it to be at least in September, but there's no reason it couldn't be done in July.”

Senate Ag Chair John Boozman (R-Ark.) told your host in a statement that he is looking forward to marking up the farm bill during this work period and “ensuring the President’s supplemental includes the funding necessary to meet the needs of farmers.”

“There's real momentum to advancing policies that help farmers, and I'm committed to working with my colleagues to make that happen,” Boozman added.

Republicans are returning to intraparty disarray after House GOP leaders canceled votes on major bills before the Fourth of July recess. After a group of GOP hard-liners derailed progress at the end of June, some Republicans questioned whether the rest of the summer will be a wash.

The unexpected death of South Carolina Republican Lindsey Graham over the weekend complicates the picture in the Senate, narrowing the already-slim GOP majority. The majority must also account for the absence of Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), who has been hospitalized for nearly a month after falling. He said Sunday that he will return to the Senate after his recovery but has not specified when.

In the lower chamber, Rep. Andy Barr (R-Ky.) is preparing to introduce a bipartisan bill on hemp regulation as soon as Tuesday that would roll back some of the language that the industry considers a ban on its products, according to two people familiar with the plan who were granted anonymity to discuss it.

A spokesperson for Barr did not respond to a request for comment.

Lawmakers supportive of the industry have scrambled to undo or delay the limitations on hemp products, which were included in the shutdown-ending funding bill passed last fall, before they go into effect this November. McConnell played a key role in pushing the restrictions through.

Then there’s House Ag Chair G.T. Thompson’s (R-Pa.) farm labor bill, which must receive Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan’s (R-Ohio) blessing to get a markup, as it must flow through his committee. Jordan told MA before the Fourth of July recess that he was undecided on whether to take up the legislation.
 

A message from Bayer:
 
AROUND THE AGENCIES

PUTTING ON THE RITZ: Rollins is slated to attend a dinner at George Washington’s Mount Vernon this evening, according to a copy of an event flyer obtained by POLITICO, Jacob writes in.

Attendees may pay from $7,500 to $15,000 to sponsor the event, according to the flyer.

For $15,000, a sponsor can get a table of 12 at the event, prominent name placement on promotional materials and “tailored branding input, including opportunities to provide digital content.”

The event will celebrate 250 years of American agriculture and its future and is co-hosted by Mount Vernon Ladies’ Association.

A digital form for sponsorship pledges linked in the event flyer states that “an ‘Ag250 Sponsor Invoice’ will follow with payment instructions to CropLife America.” CLA is a trade association representing the pesticide industry.

“CropLife America offered to be the point of coordination for the event,” CLA spokesperson Tonya Parish told MA in a statement. “The event is not designed to generate a profit, and any incidental proceeds will be donated to youth agricultural organizations and Mount Vernon.”

USDA did not respond to a request for comment about the event and CropLife’s involvement. Mount Vernon did not respond to a request for comment about the event.
 

A message from Bayer:

At Bayer, we believe in delivering smarter, practical tools directly to American farmers. Through advanced digital platforms, we provide accurate, real-time data maps with insights on moisture, nutrients, and compaction. This gives farmers the information they need to unlock their soil's full potential.

We empower growers to advance regenerative agriculture, helping to secure a financially sustainable future with boosted yields.

Learn more.
 
BIOFUELS FIGHT

MA EXCLUSIVE: A new poll out today charted record-high voter support for E15 fuel and year-round E15 sales legislation.

The poll, conducted by Morning Consult for the Renewable Fuels Association, comes after the House passed a year-round nationwide E15 bill in May. The bill is now in the Senate and has stalled as lawmakers deliberate on the best path forward for it, whether as a standalone or part of an upcoming package. The legislation, iterations of which have been introduced in many congresses, has been difficult to pass due to competing ag and small oil refineries interests.

The poll found that 75 percent of registered voters surveyed backed expanding the availability of the ethanol blend and 71 percent supported federal legislation allowing its sale year-round.

“The Senate has a clear opportunity to deliver what voters want by making E15 available year-round, nationwide,” RFA President and CEO Geoff Cooper said in a statement.

“The House has already passed year-round E15 legislation, and President Trump has repeatedly called on Congress to make this a priority,” he added.

item.title: ‘It's going to decimate the agency’
item.content:encoded:
Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin

With help from Marcia Brown and Oliver Ward

The Agriculture Department is undergoing a sweeping reorganization. | Getty Images
QUICK FIX

— Agriculture Department employees continue to warn that a massive reorganization plan will degrade the quality of their work.

— Ag representatives are set to join U.S. trade negotiators in Mexico this week as bilateral U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement review talks continue.

— A Democratic senator plans to introduce a pair of bills targeting consolidation in the ag economy and wage standards.

IT’S MONDAY, JULY 20. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send pitches to rshin@politico.com. Contact me securely on Signal to share tips at rshin.80. Follow us at @Morning_Ag for more.

BIG CHANGES AT PLAYBOOK: Starting today, ADAM WREN, DASHA BURNS and WILL STEAKIN become co-authors of POLITICO's flagship morning newsletter, with an official relaunch set for Aug. 31. Burns will also anchor a refreshed Playbook Podcast, and MEGAN MESSERLY will join Playbook as a contributor to the newsletter and podcast. Read more here.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
DRIVING THE DAY

INTERNAL UNEASE: USDA employees say major programs, including international food aid and agriculture research, could break down due to a department reorganization that is relocating many USDA jobs across the country.

Collin Bradley, president of the AFSCME Local 3976 union that represents Foreign Agricultural Service workers, told MA the billions of dollars that flow through Food for Peace — the United States' international food aid program — are “going to be managed by less than 10 people who are staying in D.C.”

“Foreign service officers are going to be pretty screwed” as well, he said, because of the relocation of the Global Services branch that manages operations for U.S. embassies abroad.

FAS workers were told Friday that more than one-third of them have been asked to relocate, Marcia reported.

Food safety groups and experts separately asked Ag Secretary Brooke Rollins on Friday to pause the proposed department’s relocation of its Environmental Microbial and Food Safety Laboratory out of the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center.

“The loss of highly specialized scientific expertise would be substantial,” the experts wrote in a letter. “Past USDA relocations have shown that such moves often result in significant staff attrition, leading to gaps in institutional knowledge and reduced effectiveness in serving agricultural stakeholders.”

Workers in other USDA agencies similarly worried that the quality of the department’s work could be a shadow of itself once the restructuring is complete.

“It's just bad for agricultural research, and everybody is just really in a bad place mentally,” said an Agricultural Research Service employee, granted anonymity to discuss the internal mood.

USDA rejected that the reorganization would be detrimental to research.

“The Department has made clear the reorganization is a regimented, multi-step process, and that specific to research, all continues without interruption, except the research Congress chose to defund,” USDA spokesperson Michael Abboud said in a statement.

Both ag research and foreign service employees are predicting high attrition that could wipe out expertise.

FAS conducted a survey that found only 4 percent of people said they would relocate to Kansas City, Missouri — the hub where USDA is reassigning most of the agency, according to Bradley.

“It's going to decimate the agency,” Bradley told MA.

MA readers will recall: A coalition of unions and other groups renewed efforts to halt the reorganization, citing documents showing that USDA expects nearly a quarter of its employees to quit rather than relocate.

The reorganization was intended to reduce USDA's workforce “by approximately 23,177 which is a 23% overall reduction,” according to the 2025 internal planning documents.
TRADE TALKS

ON THE LAMB: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer held a roundtable with sheep producers on trade policy in Utah Friday following his directive last week to the International Trade Commission to investigate the impact of lamb imports on the domestic industry.

Carson Jorgensen, sheep producer and former chair of the Utah Republican Party, hosted Greer at Skyline Sheep Company and accompanied him on a tour of public lands used for grazing.

“[Greer] had a very specific interest in agriculture and manufacturing,” Jorgensen told MA Sunday. “They want people to come back and bring manufacturing jobs back to the United States, and they want to protect domestic agriculture, and they were very bullish on the trade deficit.”

The ITC will determine whether imports are causing injury to American producers. If so, it will make recommendations for redress, which could include tariffs.

Lamb and mutton imports from New Zealand and Australia had secured over 70 percent of the U.S. market as of 2024, according to the American Sheep Industry Association.

Jorgensen and a group of other sheep industry advocates submitted a letter to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative in early 2025 urging it to launch the investigation into foreign lamb imports.

Jorgensen said Greer has been “pretty vocal since the beginning that he's in favor of these tariffs.”

ROUND THREE: Representatives from multiple U.S. industries will be heading to Mexico this week with trade negotiators as bilateral talks on the USMCA review advance, Oliver writes in.

Industries including agriculture and steel will be represented among the delegation, according to four people familiar with the plans, granted anonymity because they were not cleared to brief the media on the closed-door discussions.

The details: Greer will meet with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Secretary of the Economy Marcelo Ebrard during his three-day visit to Mexico City, which begins Wednesday, according to USTR. Among the topics the two sides are looking to discuss are steel and aluminum derivatives, labor and agriculture.

The Trump administration is expected to leave the statutory text of the agreement unchanged to avoid having Congress vote on changes to the deal, preferring to use interpretive agreements, annexes or side letters to make adjustments.

It has, however, shared some portions of texts under discussions with relevant industries, two of the people familiar with the plans told Morning Trade.

The text goes beyond written demands, one of them said, calling it “legalese.”

“It's actual negotiating text that would be part of the agreement that gets signed,” they added.

Meanwhile, Canada continues to take flak, with President Donald Trump issuing another tariff threat Friday, this time over the dangerous air quality in U.S. cities caused by Canadian wildfires.

“We are holding Canada responsible for the fact that they are not properly maintaining their Forests, and Brush therein,” Trump posted on Truth Social Friday, suggesting the cost of pollution will be “added to the tariffs.”
ON THE HILL

MA EXCLUSIVE: Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.) is set to introduce a pair of bills that aim to weaken consolidation in the ag market and set new standards for wages and working conditions for food companies that do business with the federal government.

Sens. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) co-sponsored the Fairness for Small-Scale Farmers and Ranchers Act, which would enact a moratorium on future corporate mergers of big food and ag companies. The bill would also reinstate mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef.

The Agricultural Worker Justice Act, co-sponsored by Booker, Sanders and Sens. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), would prohibit USDA from buying meat, poultry or processed food made by workers paid below the prevailing wage rate in their area. It directs the Labor Department to determine prevailing rates.

“Rapid consolidation has jeopardized the well-being and vitality of farms across America — we can’t let that happen,” Welch said in a statement. “We also need urgent, commonsense safeguards to protect workers in the agricultural industry who face hazardous and exploitative working conditions.”
PROPOSITION 12

MA EXCLUSIVE PART 1: More than 700 veterinarians sent a letter to members of Congress urging them to keep the Save Our Bacon Act out of the farm bill and other legislative vehicles.

The Save Our Bacon Act would roll back California’s Proposition 12, which sets standards for animal confinement for food products sold in the state. It was included in the House-passed version of the farm bill but left out of the Senate’s version.

“This harmful legislation would strip states and localities of their rights to pass a wide range of measures protecting animal welfare and public health,” the veterinarians wrote.

The letter was organized by Humane Veterinary Medical Alliance, the veterinary division of Humane World for Animals.

MA EXCLUSIVE PART 2: A July poll out of Iowa found that nearly twice as many voters oppose the Save Our Bacon Act as support it.

The poll of 625 registered Iowa voters took place earlier this month. It was conducted by Mason-Dixon Polling and Strategy and commissioned by the Defeat EATS coalition.

In every congressional district in Iowa except the 4th District, more voters said they oppose the law than support it, the poll found.

Democrats were more likely than Republicans to oppose the bill, and 53 percent of independents said they opposed it.
Industry Intel

UNO REVERSE: Bayer is withdrawing its request that the Trump administration impose countervailing duties on glyphosate imports from China after backlash from the agriculture industry, as our Grace Yarrow reported.

The parent company of pesticide giant Monsanto filed a petition last month with the Commerce Department’s International Trade Administration and the U.S. International Trade Commission, arguing that Chinese competitors benefit from unfair pricing that hurts U.S.-based glyphosate producers including its Ruveon subsidiary.

“Since filing our petitions, we have engaged directly with farmers and agricultural trade associations to hear their perspectives,” Ruveon said in a statement Friday announcing the retraction of the petition. “Today's decision reflects our commitment to putting farmers first and meeting their evolving needs, especially during this challenging farm economy.”

Read more from Grace here.
Row Crops

— Democrats see an opening in rural states for the first time in decades. In Iowa, it’s about water, Tom Philpott and Nina B. Elkadi report for POLITICO Magazine.

— Seafood Supply Co., a Dallas seafood wholesaler, was sentenced to pay a $250,000 fine for falsifying the country of origin for its salmon.

— Taylor Farms is recalling its Mexican-grown iceberg lettuce from the U.S. after American authorities linked the lettuce to a parasitic outbreak. (The Wall Street Journal)

— The Independent Beef Association of North Dakota sent a letter to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission in opposition to the agency’s new Beef Trim futures and options contracts, saying that the contracts “will place a fictitious value on beef trim.”

item.title: Wavering on SNAP waivers
item.content:encoded:
Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin

With help from Grace Yarrow and Marcia Brown

SNAP waivers are one of the flagship policy achievements of the Trump administration’s USDA and HHS. | AP
QUICK FIX

— An absence of congressional energy around junk food restrictions in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program is dimming the initiative’s once-bright future.

— The Trump administration will resume cattle imports on the southern border amid the New World screwworm outbreak.

— Over 20 lawmakers wrote to Deputy Agriculture Secretary Stephen Vaden to voice worries about the Agriculture Department’s Rural Development reorganization.

IT’S MONDAY, JULY 27. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send pitches to rshin@politico.com. Send me tips securely on Signal at rshin.80. Follow us at @Morning_Ag for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
DRIVING THE DAY

LOSING STEAM: A lack of political will in Congress to codify a signature Make America Healthy Again initiative is casting doubt on whether it can survive its latest legal roadblock.

SNAP waivers, which limit the purchase of unhealthy foods like candy and soda with the federal benefits, are one of the flagship policy achievements of the Trump administration’s Department of Agriculture and Department of Health and Human Services. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. even linked states’ rural health funding to applications for the waivers.

But a federal judge tossed out the restrictions for five states — Colorado, Iowa, Nebraska, Tennessee and West Virginia — in June, jeopardizing the initiative’s future.

MAHA-aligned lawmakers still support the idea of limiting SNAP purchases to items seen as healthy, but there’s little resolve to legislate on the issue at the federal level. Critics of the program’s current state-by-state form say it has established a patchwork of rules, arguing federal action is needed to eliminate inconsistency throughout the country.

Senate Ag Chair John Boozman (R-Ark.) said he has no interest in floating such a ban in the farm bill, for which changes to SNAP are already a key party-line division.

“What we're trying to do is pass the farm bill, and we really need to get the votes together to get that passed — and that’s probably not something that would help,” Boozman told MA. “It’s very controversial, and it's not really partisan. It just divides both Democrats and Republicans. I don't know that there's really any consensus about it.

“Something else might come up, other legislation later in the year, but for now, we're trying to stay away from it in the farm bill,” Boozman told MA.

Members of the Senate MAHA Caucus have remained supportive of the policy but don’t have concrete plans to try to make it law. Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.) said he was open to introducing a measure in Congress because the state waiver system was blocked in several states.

“If that's the only way to get it done, we need to get people on real food, not processed food,” Tuberville told MA.

Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) similarly said he is all for SNAP waivers.

“I think that’s a reasonable restriction, when the federal government is providing benefits to people, to restrict what you can spend that money on,” Johnson told MA. “This case would be a win-win because not only would it be cheaper, but it'd be healthier.”

But he said right now, there is “probably not” bandwidth to introduce a bill on such a policy.

Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) proposed a junk food ban amendment to Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.)’s Childhood Diabetes Reduction Act. The legislation would already add warning labels to added-sugar or ultra-processed foods.

But Senate MAHA Caucus founder Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) voted to table the amendment despite being “truly torn,” saying he thought adding it would tank Sanders’ labeling legislation.

“It's absolutely a tough call on what to do here,” Marshall said in the markup. “Eventually, we need to figure a way to incorporate Senator Paul's goal here as well, but … I don't think we'd have the votes to get the big bill, Senator Sanders' bill, across the finish line if it passes.”

Paul slammed the lawmakers who voted to table his amendment on social media. Paul’s and Marshall’s offices did not respond to requests for comment.

Senate HELP Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.) said he agrees with the concept of Paul’s amendment but also voted to table it due to jurisdiction, saying they needed to “consult with the Ag Committee.”
BILL WATCH

MAKE HAY WHILE THE SUN SHINES: Boozman told MA that he hopes to schedule a farm bill markup during the first week of August.

“Not next week, but the next week,” he said Thursday. “That's what we're shooting for.”

But with the Senate's recess beginning Aug. 7, senators will face a tight timeline to act.

Boozman reiterated it is important for Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) — who has been absent from Congress for over a month after he was hospitalized following a fall in June — to be present for the markup. Republicans hold just a one-vote majority on the Ag Committee.

“Senator McConnell is still not back,” Boozman said. “We'd like to have him there. He's in rehab and working hard, so hopefully we get him back.”

Where the negotiations stand: Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.) said Democrats are pushing to get a delay of “at least a couple years” for SNAP’s cost share framework that was passed in the GOP’s sweeping domestic policy law last summer.

MA readers will recall the megalaw will require most states with SNAP error rates above 6 percent to split the cost of the program with the federal government.

“Only in Washington the exemption goes to the states that had the highest rate of noncompliance,” Welch told reporters Thursday, referring to an existing carve-out that allows states with error rates above approximately 13.34 percent to delay implementation for up to two years.
Where's the beef?

OPEN ‘EM UP: USDA is lifting a ban on cattle imports from Mexico as the Trump administration aims to lower beef prices ahead of the midterm elections, two people familiar with the matter confirmed on Friday, as Grace and Marcia report.

The administration had banned imports as part of its effort to contain the New World screwworm, a flesh-eating parasite threatening U.S. livestock.

USDA later on Friday announced that it will open the Douglas, Arizona, port of entry to cattle trade on Aug. 24, while simultaneously initiating the operational steps necessary for openings at two ports in New Mexico, Santa Teresa and Columbus. No ports along the Texas border were mentioned, and the department said the ports could be closed again, if needed.

“Protecting the United States from [New World screwworm] and pushing this pest out of Mexico and back to the Darien Gap is a top priority at USDA and has the full attention of the Trump Administration,” Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said in a statement.

The move comes after Rollins had resisted pressure from Republicans and the cattle industry to open the border to help ease high prices.

“The closure of the Southern ports of entry for the last year has been a tough but necessary action to control the spread of [New World screwworm] in Mexico and protect the American livestock industry," Rollins said in her Friday statement.

The Wall Street Journal first reported that the border was set to reopen.

“Resuming cattle importation from Mexico is the right move for ranchers and American consumers, but it's a decision that should have been made sooner," Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller said in a statement Friday. "While I'm pleased to see this important trade relationship restored, the prolonged closure has already taken a toll on producers, disrupted supply chains, and created uncertainty that could have lasting consequences for the cattle industry."
ON THE HILL

MA EXCLUSIVE: Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) led over 20 lawmakers in sending a letter to Vaden on Friday expressing concerns over the Rural Development mission area’s reorganization.

The lawmakers argued the branch plays a unique role in underpinning local rural and ag economies, as it provides financing and support for several types of rural infrastructure, including housing and clinics.

They said the mission area must have worker capacity to process applications and disburse funds, noting it already lost over a third of its headcount last year. They said more attrition is anticipated through the reorganization.

They asked Vaden to respond to a series of questions on staffing and operations, including a request for a breakdown of staffing levels and projection of staffing by mission area for the next two years.

“Given the significant depletion of staff, is Rural Development hiring now or planning to recruit new staff in the next three months?” the members wrote. “If USDA anticipates hiring new staff, how will the Department ensure they receive the training needed to effectively serve rural communities with the required expertise and level of service?”

USDA did not respond to a request for comment on the letter.

MA EXCLUSIVE PART 2: Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) and Jim Justice (R-W.Va.) are set to introduce bipartisan legislation today aimed at mitigating flooding on farmland. Reps. Jimmy Panetta (D-Calif.) and Randy Feenstra (R-Iowa) will introduce companion legislation in the House.

The Farmers Lifeline Options for Overcoming Disasters Act would increase access to voluntary floodplain easements for rural communities, helping farmers before weather events take place.

“Our farming communities are key to both our culture and economy,” Blunt Rochester said in a statement. “Which is why I’m proud to introduce the FLOOD Act to ensure farmers in the First State and across the country have the resources they need to protect their properties, their crops, and their livelihoods.”

Feenstra said in a statement that the FLOOD Act would help the ag economy “emerge stronger and more resilient after disaster strikes.”
Row Crops

— Former FDA Deputy Commissioner Frank Yiannas called for an independent after-the-fact review of how the federal government has handled the record-breaking cyclospora outbreak, Marcia reports.

— Rollins, Georgia Ag Commissioner Tyler Harper and Rep. Brian Jack (R-Ga.) will tour a sod farm and hold a press conference in Georgia today to announce an agreement between USDA and the Georgia Department of Agriculture.

— The Commodity Futures Trading Commission will hold its first Agricultural Advisory Committee meeting of 2026 on Wednesday.

— The Forest Service remains stretched on the Sawtooth National Recreation Area in Idaho, a place with ties to key agency leaders, and is leaning on volunteer groups for help, Marc Heller of POLITICO’s E&E News reports.

— Americans are rewiring their grocery shopping routines while digesting the biggest price jump in 50 years. (The Associated Press)

THAT’S ALL FOR MA! Drop us a line and send us your agriculture job announcements or events: gyarrow@politico.com, marciabrown@politico.com, rshin@politico.com, jperez@politico.com and gmott@politico.com.
