item.content:encoded:
Presented by Danone: Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin

Presented by 

With help from Oliver Ward

“People talk about helping the farm community and rural America,” Senate Ag Chair John Boozman (R-Ark.) said. “Now is a chance to match the rhetoric with a vote and support of a very good farm bill.” | Francis Chung/E&E News
QUICK FIX

— A key Democrat on the Senate Ag Committee is urging his colleagues to withhold support for the farm bill despite concessions intended to sweeten the legislation for Democrats.

— Though President Donald Trump’s tariffs may have cost U.S. ag producers billions in lost exports over a one-year period, many farm-state lawmakers still welcome using tariffs as a statecraft tool.

— Industry groups are launching a full-court press to influence Proposition 12’s fate in the farm bill.

IT’S MONDAY, AUG. 3. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Buckle up for a wild last week in session before recess, and don’t forget to read your favorite team’s reporting to stay on top of farm bill news. Send pitches to rshin@politico.com and contact me on Signal at rshin.80. Follow us at @Morning_Ag for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
 

A message from Danone:

Healthy communities start with a strong food system. That's why Danone USA partners with family farms across America to source ingredients for its nutrient dense food and beverages. We invest in the people and practices that help farms thrive for generations to come. From advancing regenerative agriculture to enhancing manufacturing and nutrition innovation, we're working to bring health through food to as many people as possible, while helping to build a more resilient future of food. Learn more.
 
DRIVING THE DAY

FIRST UP: Senate appropriators released text Sunday of a stopgap funding bill to avert a shutdown come Oct. 1 and punt broader government funding negotiations until after the midterms, as our colleagues Jennifer Scholtes and Katherine Tully-McManus reported.

The continuing resolution includes a delay for the effective ban on hemp products that was set to take effect in November. The regulations would hit only purely synthetic cannabinoids until Dec. 11, the CR's expiration date, and everything else would stay legal under the old rules.

SEASON FINALE: Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) launched the first salvo against Senate Agriculture Committee Chair John Boozman’s (R-Ark.) farm bill, rallying his party against the legislation despite its inclusion of a food aid compromise.

“The Republican Farm Bill released on Friday fails to meet the moment of crisis facing America's farmers and families,” Booker told MA in a statement. “Democrats should remain united and only support a Farm Bill that includes a clean two-year delay of the SNAP cost shift to states.”

The New Jersey Democrat added that the bill must also provide “immediate, meaningful assistance” for small and midsized farmers, including livestock, dairy, fruit and vegetable producers.

Booker’s call for his colleagues to oppose the bill is a blow to Boozman, who needs bipartisan support in Thursday’s planned markup, accounting for Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-Ky.) absence from Congress following a fall in June.

The text represents the culmination of the chair’s long negotiating effort aimed at crafting legislation that satisfies enough parties to clear committee and reach the Senate’s 60-vote threshold. Boozman’s package would afford states a one-year delay of an error rate-based requirement to share the cost of providing Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits.

Committee Democrats had previously said they wouldn’t vote for the bill unless it affords states two years before the cost-share requirement takes effect, which Booker doubled down on. Ranking member Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) told MA in a statement that she and Boozman “are continuing to discuss the bill that members received.”

“I look forward to working on the details of a bipartisan Farm Bill that can pass on the Senate floor as it will need both Republican and Democratic support,” Klobuchar said. “Senate Ag Democrats have been clear that a Farm Bill must meet the needs of both farmers and families across America.”

In response to Democratic pushback, Boozman told MA in a statement that his bill “reflects a compromise supported by Republicans and the White House” and “it’s hard to see any better deal coming together.”

“People talk about helping the farm community and rural America,” the chair added. “Now is a chance to match the rhetoric with a vote and support of a very good farm bill.”

Left-of-center groups said the farm bill’s one-year delay isn’t sufficient to draw their support.

“Chair Boozman’s farm bill proposal falls short on SNAP, despite including a step in the right direction, and further changes are needed before the legislation moves forward,” Sharon Parrott, president of the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, posted on X.

“States would get more time to budget for the cost shift,” Parrott added. “But it will still be based on error rates for this fiscal year, which is nearly over.”

Environmental Working Group Senior Vice President of Government Affairs Scott Faber similarly said in a statement that the farm bill falls short by “failing to restore the cuts to SNAP that have left more than 1 million children without anti-hunger assistance.”

But some ag industry groups were elated that an ethanol measure was included in the Senate farm bill text. The year-round E15 provision could have bipartisan draw as ag-state lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have said it would be a boon for farmers.

“We are extremely grateful that year-round E15 continues to be part of the conversation,” National Corn Growers Association President Jed Bower said in a statement. “This is a top priority for corn growers, who greatly need expanded sources of demand, like the kind year-round E15 would offer.”

MA readers will recall there has been a yearslong effort to allow the sale of E15 nationwide permanently.

Additional context: Boozman’s package would create a steeper penalty for states with the highest SNAP error payment rates, requiring states with error rates above 6 percent to pay for 20 percent of benefits — instead of the 15 percent maximum a state would have to contribute under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act guidelines — starting in fiscal 2031.

The E15 provision is a version of a bill the House passed in May with refiner-friendly language that mirrors legislation championed by Sens. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) and Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.).
 

A message from Danone:
 
TRADE CORNER

TOOLS OF THE TRADE: Farmers and ranchers have been on the front lines of the U.S. trade war with China and were rocked by steep retaliatory tariffs last year that slashed exports to one of their largest buyers. But after more than a year of heightened export uncertainty, farm-state lawmakers say they still see room for higher tariffs on China and welcome their use as a statecraft tool, Oliver writes in.

The details: A Russia sanctions bill proposed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham is inching through the Senate, with its architects hoping to pass the legislation before the August recess begins at the end of the week.

The bill would give the president new powers to adopt tariffs of up to 500 percent on Russia and up to 100 percent on countries helping Moscow evade sanctions and the five largest buyers of Russian energy — including its top customer, China. Trump last week also argued the bill should be updated to include a similar provision for buyers of Iranian oil.

The tariff provisions are getting some heat. Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) has introduced an amendment to strip the tariff language from the bill, which is drawing some Democratic backing.

“We should use every lever possible,” Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa) said. “Leaving [the bill] as is would allow the president to make that decision.”

Sen. John Hoeven (R-N.D.) made a similar argument.

“We're trying to deter Russia continuing to fight Ukraine. We're trying to deter Russia and China from helping Iran,” he said. The proposed tariff measures, he argued, give Trump the “discretion to do what needs to be done.”

Remember: Chinese retaliatory tariffs last year, which peaked at 125 percent on U.S. exports, cost U.S. ag producers almost $15 billion in lost exports over a one-year period, according to an analysis from North Dakota State University.

Soybean producers, which relied on China for around half of their exports, were hit particularly hard, suffering export losses of nearly $7 billion, according to the analysis. Ernst’s Iowa was also among the states most affected, with $1.2 billion in lost exports, along with Illinois and California.

Trump has long argued tariffs are necessary to confront China’s trade practices and balance U.S. trade deficits. But since returning to office, he has widened the scope of issues he is willing to use duties to address, ranging from immigration to fentanyl, foreign policy and the prosecution of his political allies abroad.

Election season: An ag lobbyist, granted anonymity to describe closed-door conversations with lawmakers and aides, told POLITICO that some farm-state lawmakers are more skeptical in private about the utility of tariffs to advance policy goals outside the trade realm.

“It's a mixed bag,” the lobbyist said. “Some of them understand that tariffs have been used and utilized in a way that's really backfired on the agricultural economy.”

But the lobbyist noted that just three months from the midterms, few are willing to break publicly with Trump on the issue.

“The conversation may be different after November,” they said.

It's not only Republicans who seem comfortable with using tariffs as a punitive tool to advance non-trade aims.

Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) defended the tariff measures in the sanctions bill.

“It's a targeted tariff that focuses on holding Russia accountable and prevents, and rightfully so, those five countries from providing any support or any fossil fuel revenue to Russia,” she told POLITICO. “China needs to be held accountable.”
 

A message from Danone:

Strong agriculture. Better food. Healthier communities.

For nearly 85 years, Danone USA has produced food and beverages for communities and consumers across America, made possible by a network of local producer-partners spanning the country. Today, our business relies on an interconnected American food system. From family farms and domestic ingredient sourcing to manufacturing and nutrition science, every step depends on long-term investment and partnership.

Danone sources ~90% of its ingredients domestically and works with dozens of producer-partners across the country to help advance regenerative agriculture and support farm resiliency. We actively invest in our farm partners to fortify the future of food so we can continue creating our nutrient-dense food and beverages for Americans.

The result is a model built on shared success: supporting agriculture, advancing nutrition, and creating lasting value for communities nationwide.

See how Danone is helping build a stronger future through food.
 
PROPOSITION 12

MA EXCLUSIVE PART 1: Humane World Action Fund is rolling out a six-figure ad buy today opposing the Save Our Bacon Act, preceding the expected Thursday markup of the farm bill.

The $250,000 buy in the Minnesota market urges voters to push lawmakers to exclude language that would preempt California’s Proposition 12, which sets animal confinement standards for food products sold in the state. The Save Our Bacon Act, which would overturn Proposition 12, was included in the House-passed version of the farm bill but was left out of the Senate’s text.

“The Senate has an opportunity to keep the Farm Bill focused on helping farmers navigate the real challenges facing agriculture, not providing a special favor to a handful of corporate pork interests that have spent years trying to overturn laws they couldn’t defeat at the ballot box or in the courts,” said Sara Amundson, president of Humane World Action Fund, in a statement.

MA EXCLUSIVE PART 2: The Center for the Environment and Welfare, an animal ag advocacy group that opposes Proposition 12, conducted polling in seven states and found support in each market for passing a preemption of Proposition 12.

CEW surveyed residents of Delaware, Alaska, Colorado, Utah, Minnesota, Wisconsin and Virginia. Over half of those surveyed in each state said they wanted their representatives to support a preemption.

The survey’s questions framed the policy as a law that “caused the prices of pork and eggs nationwide to go up.”

The polling was done as part of CEW’s “Food Price Fix” campaign, which advocates for Congress to roll back Proposition 12.

MA EXCLUSIVE PART 3: A new economic analysis commissioned by the American Meat Producers Association, an advocacy group that supports Proposition 12, estimated that hundreds of millions of dollars invested by farmers could be lost if the California regulation is preempted.

Producers have invested an estimated $483 million to $696 million nationwide to bring operations in line with Proposition 12 standards through renovations and construction, according to the report, and about 90 percent of that investment would be “potentially stranded” if the law is rolled back.

“We made those investments because the law was settled and the courts upheld it,” Brent Hershey, a Pennsylvania hog farmer, said in a statement. “Pulling that away now unfairly punishes farmers who did the responsible thing while rewarding the biggest operators who didn't.”
Row Crops

— Exclusive: A new fact sheet by conservation advocacy group Invest in Our Land lays out talking points on how the farm bill would cut $1.92 billion from the Environmental Quality Incentives Program from fiscal 2027 to fiscal 2030.

— Exclusive: The National Grocers Association sent a letter to the Senate Ag Committee Friday encouraging the lawmakers to establish an “implementation transition period for the new SNAP benefit cost-share requirements.”

— The Trump administration took a cautious approach to managing the Colorado River, but it still might spark a legal melee, Annie Snider of POLITICO’s E&E News reports.

— USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service is enhancing its residue program’s methods of surveilling veterinary drugs used to treat New World screwworm in livestock.

Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Marcia Brown

With help from Grace Yarrow and Sophie Gardner
QUICK FIX

— Americans are still afraid to eat lettuce and other fresh produce amid the nation’s worst recorded cyclospora season. That’s making it harder for Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to advance his “Eat Real Food” message.

— The Senate Agriculture Committee chair is calling on farmers and ranchers to pressure Democrats to pass a farm bill.

— FIRST IN MA: A new bipartisan bill would regulate hemp-derived THC beverages like alcohol.

IT’S MONDAY, AUG. 10. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Marcia Brown and I was delighted to learn that peaches are healthy and delicious. Send pitches to marciabrown@politico.com and contact me on Signal at marciagbrown.68. Follow us at @Rachel_Shin_, @YarrowGrace and @Marcia_Brown9 for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
DRIVING THE DAY

CYCLOSPORA: Kennedy’s call for Americans to “eat real food” to combat chronic illness is being tested by a parasite that’s driving consumers away from fresh produce, your host and Sophie Gardner report.

The spread of cyclospora, a parasite that can cause explosive diarrhea, is prompting people to reconsider their fresh food choices just as Kennedy launches a cooking show to spread his healthy eating message.

A recent poll found that 40 percent of Americans say they’re buying or eating less produce and retailers are already feeling the impact.

“HHS is simultaneously telling Americans to eat more fresh produce and warning that eating the wrong fresh produce — without being able to tell people which — puts them at risk of severe, prolonged diarrhea,” Jerome Adams, who served as surgeon general during President Donald Trump’s first term, said in an email. “That mixed message is not abstract. It is scaring people away from salads and other fresh foods right now — the exact opposite of the ‘eat real food’ goal.”

The record number of cyclospora cases in the current season — more than doubling the previous record — has led some health experts and consumers to question whether federal cuts to staffing, surveillance and funding for states may be to blame. It’s also revived long-running concerns across several administrations about the federal government’s failure to finalize new food safety measures — even as many food safety experts and nutritionists agree that Americans should be eating more fruits and vegetables.

Frank Yiannas, the Food and Drug Administration’s top food safety official during Trump’s first term, criticized a “lack of clear, timely communication about which products were implicated, which were not, and what actions consumers could take to protect themselves” from cyclospora. That created a vacuum where misinformation and fear led to “reduced consumer confidence in the very foods we want people to eat more of — fresh fruits and vegetables,” he wrote in a text message.

HHS response: Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson from the Department of Health and Human Services, defended the agency’s response, saying the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the FDA have “communicated actively throughout this investigation.”

“That outreach has included official social media updates, continuously updated outbreak webpages, and ongoing engagement with the news media,” Hilliard said in a statement.

White House adviser Calley Means pushed back after this story’s original publication, noting that Stop Foodborne Illness — a nonprofit led by former Biden administration official Sandra Eskin, who was among those criticizing the administration’s response — receives food industry funding.

“Whenever you read about the cyclospora outbreak, please know that junk food companies are paying millions of dollars to spur this hysteria to get you to eat less real food,” he wrote on X.

Stop Foodborne Illness, which works with consumers and food companies, advocates stricter food safety regulations.

“STOP Foodborne illness, which has worked tirelessly for decades to improve the safety of the food supply, wants consumers to eat more fresh produce,” Eskin told MA in a statement Sunday. “When more than 20,000 people are getting sick from it, however, there is a problem that needs to be fixed.”

Outbreak latest: In Michigan, which appears to be the epicenter of the outbreak, case numbers indicate it could be slowing down. But this year’s caseload tops any previous record and has prompted some to call for an after-the-fact review of the outbreak and the federal government’s response.

And of course, cyclospora isn’t the only thing sickening people lately.

The CDC is investigating a salmonella outbreak linked to jalapeno peppers that has sickened more than 300 people across 27 states. The Department of Agriculture’s Food Safety and Inspection Service also issued a public health alert for meat and poultry products that may contain the peppers.

Check out the full list of current foodborne illness investigations the FDA is undertaking here.
farm bill

FUTURE OF FARM BILL: Senate Ag Committee Chair John Boozman (R-Ark.) is urging farmers and ranchers to pressure Democrats to come to the table on the farm bill after it failed to advance last week.

“[Farmers] need to show up at their meetings and say, ‘You voted against this. We expect you to vote for it,’” he told reporters Friday. “‘Come September, we desperately need the help. Work out your other problems.’”

Boozman said lawmakers will reconvene on the farm bill in September and that he will keep in touch with ranking member Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) during recess.

“They're moving so far left. They're in the middle of their primaries, and they’re very careful about voting for anything,” he said. “I don’t care what the issue is — they don’t want to appear that they are helping Republicans, which is really sad.”

Context: Democrats called for a two-year delay to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program’s benefits cost-share provision, which Republicans enacted in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year. The provision, which will impose billions in new costs on states, is contributing to declining participation among income-eligible people, anti-hunger advocates and state officials say.

Governors from both parties have also called for a two-year delay, arguing the new costs could force states to take drastic steps, including dropping out of SNAP entirely.

GOP lawmakers offered a compromise of a one-year delay in the farm bill. But that didn’t satisfy Senate Democrats, who say they want all states “on the same footing” to reduce error rates.

Still, Boozman told reporters that the “vast majority of my conference” and the White House don’t support the two-year proposal from Democrats.

What’s next: Lawmakers will reconvene next month, but it’s not clear either party is ready to budge. However, if Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) returns to the Senate, that will give Republicans enough votes to advance the bill without Democratic support.

Boozman told reporters he’s still “unsure of timing” around McConnell’s return.

“I can't tell you, you know, when that's his business, and he needs to work that out and I support it,” he said. “But hopefully, we'll get him back soon.”

Subscribe free.

 
 
ON THE HILL

ARE YOU 21? Reps. Beth Van Duyne (R-Texas) and Greg Landsman (D-Ohio) are planning to introduce the Beverage Regulatory Parity Act, according to details first shared with MA.

The legislation would regulate hemp-derived THC beverages like alcohol and create a federal regulatory pathway for the drinks. It would designate the beverages as its own adult category and have safety, labeling, distribution and enforcement standards.

The bill would also ban high-dose, synthetic products and create a 5 mg cap on total intoxicating THC per serving.

““It’s time that Congress actually regulates instead of creating an opportunity … for these beverages to be sold on a black market,” Van Duyne told MA in an interview Sunday, noting that the hemp industry reached $28 billion in sales last year, $240 million of which was hemp beverages.

Van Duyne expressed optimism about getting the bill passed this year, adding that the White House has called for a “framework” to keep the industry alive.

The legislation is also endorsed by the Wine & Spirits Wholesalers of America, which praised the bill for moving the beverages out of “a legal gray area.”

The bill preserves states’ ability to regulate, tax or even ban the products.

Reminder: The legislation comes as a federal hemp ban nears. The continuing resolution Congress passed includes a one-month extension of the ban, now set to take effect Dec. 11. The White House pushed hard for the extension over the objections of some Senate Republicans.

RURAL DEVELOPMENT: The Senate confirmed Glen Smith as USDA undersecretary for rural development as part of an en bloc vote Friday.

Hailing from Iowa, Smith most recently has served on the Farm Credit Administration’s board of directors.

The Senate Ag Committee advanced his nomination out of committee in June on a party-line vote after a monthslong delay.

A selection of canned THC drinks at Hemp House | Paul Demko/POLITICO
QUICK FIX

— The hemp industry is trying to build on the delay of a ban on its products to win a permanent regulatory framework.

— A state-owned Moroccan fertilizer manufacturer has returned to the U.S. market after the Trump administration suspended countervailing duties.

POLITICO Surge launches August 31 with reporting and analysis on rising power demand, AI infrastructure, electrification, grid constraints and the politics shaping energy’s next chapter.

Subscribe Now.

 
 
DRIVING THE DAY

AROUND THE CLOCK: There’s no rest for the weary in the hemp lobby.

After the industry eked out a buzzer-beater win by protecting a hemp ban delay in the Senate’s continuing resolution — due in large part to the White House’s intervention — lobbyists say they’re using summer break to harness momentum for the fall.

“The hemp industry does not have an August recess,” Christopher Lackner, president and CEO of the Hemp Beverage Alliance, told MA. “We’re going to continue pushing and getting ready for when Congress is back in session in September to hit the ground running.”

“We continue to activate our membership — they are all scheduling meetings in district with their representatives in August, and we anticipate having a hill climb the week of Sept. 14,” Lackner said.

MA readers will recall that the August continuing resolution, which if passed will avert a shutdown come Oct. 1, includes a delay for the effective ban on hemp products that was set to take effect in November.

Under the stopgap, those regulations — which were passed as part of the deal to end the 2025 government shutdown — would hit only purely synthetic cannabinoids until Dec. 11, the CR's expiration date. Everything else would stay legal under the old rules.

Other lobbyists who spoke with MA emphasized the need for the industry to unify behind a regulatory proposal, as well as to meet with lawmakers over break to rally support for the House’s vote on the stopgap’s provision. The fall will be an existential moment for the industry — whose companies generate billions of dollars and employ hundreds of thousands of workers — as it stares down collapse without a Hail Mary.

Jonathan Miller, general counsel of the U.S. Hemp Roundtable, said he is optimistic that House members who disagree with the hemp delay will not want to shut down the government over it.

“We're going to do everything we can to ensure that the CR passes the House as well intact,” Miller said. “And also just as importantly, developing a game plan for December so that by the time this ban expires … we're not asking for another extension, but rather, we're going to put in place meaningful regulatory reform.”

Thomas Winstanley, president of Edibles.com, a platform that sells hemp-derived drinks, gummies and other products, said he is working to activate hemp consumers as a constituency now that they are “aware of this threat.” He said the lobby’s job is now to identify a policy framework that stakeholders can get behind that is also feasible to pass within the tight deadline.

“What we're trying to do is use our sphere of influence to facilitate a lot of the dialog around what we think is a proper pathway forward, that will meet the White House's expectations and also dissuade some of the concerns that are rightfully held by members of Congress today,” Winstanley told your host.

Proponents of the restrictions passed last November have argued they would prevent the unregulated sale of intoxicants.

Winstanley said drawing from existing regulatory frameworks that the Food and Drug Administration has for products like supplements or from the model of the Treasury Department bureau that regulates and collects taxes on alcohol and tobacco is “a very realistic pathway” for hemp.

“Part of where the White House has been very clear and unwavering is that they've been sending messages of what they expect to see in terms of regulatory clarity and certainty,” Winstanley said. “The White House wants to see industry alignment on any vehicles to move forward.”

Subscribe free.

 
 
TRADE CORNER

WE'RE SO BACK: Morocco’s state-owned OCP has returned to the U.S. phosphate fertilizer market after President Donald Trump suspended countervailing duties on the company in June, a spokesperson told POLITICO on Friday, with its first shipment already landing in New Orleans.

The president declared an emergency earlier this summer arguing that constrained fertilizer supply threatened America’s agricultural production and food security. Accordingly, he lifted the more than 16 percent countervailing duties applied to OCP that had been keeping the Moroccan phosphate fertilizer giant from exporting to the U.S.

The company told Oliver that 54,000 metric tons arrived in the U.S., the first shipment since the duties were lifted.

Why it matters: Phosphate fertilizer prices have been rising since February and are heading into the late summer planting season higher than at any point in the last two years, according to Agriculture Department data, driven in large part by lingering supply chain disruptions in the Middle East affecting the availability of key fertilizer inputs, like sulfur. Agriculture groups have been pressing the administration to take steps to bolster domestic supply.

OCP North America said in a statement that while it welcomes the temporary tariff relief, “greater long-term certainty” would better support investment in its U.S. offerings and “help ensure adequate fertilizer supply for American farmers over time.”
AROUND THE AGENCIES

PARASITE: The FDA added Maine and Massachusetts to the outbreak of cyclospora cases linked to lettuce sold by Taylor Farms on Thursday. The 17-state outbreak has sickened nearly 10,000 people, and the investigation is ongoing.

The parasite, which can cause severe gastrointestinal illness, has historically been linked to fresh produce like lettuce, herbs and berries.

While cyclospora sickens people every summer, this year’s caseload more than doubles the previous record.

The FDA sent inspectors to Taylor Farms’ operations in Mexico for the first time last week, as earlier reported by The Washington Post.

“FDA has initiated an onsite inspection and sampling at Taylor Farms de Mexico in coordination with Mexican officials,” the agency wrote in its release. “FDA remains confident that all recalled iceberg lettuce related to this specific Cyclospora outbreak is off the market.”
Transitions

The Animal Health Institute appointed Marie Bucko as its first chief operating officer. Bucko joins AHI from Merck Animal Health, where she served as executive director of global public policy and multilateral engagement.

— Bipartisan, bicameral members of Congress sent letters in support of Undersecretary for Trade and Foreign Agricultural Affairs Luke Lindberg’s candidacy to lead the World Food Programme.

Presented by Working Forests Initiative: Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Marcia Brown and Rachel Shin

Presented by 

With help from Oliver Ward and Grace Yarrow

More than 17,000 people have been sickened by cyclospora this summer, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. | CDC/AP
QUICK FIX

— The defunding of cyclospora research projects is expected to hinder progress at a time when consumers are increasingly worried about the safety of the food supply.

— The Trump administration’s efforts to ease prices for farmers have overlooked metal tariffs on essential agricultural vehicles, industry representatives say.

— The White House is looking to ease beef processing regulations.

DRIVING THE DAY

RESEARCH SLASHED: The Trump administration is shuttering research projects key to the federal government’s fight against cyclospora, the foodborne parasite sickening thousands of Americans this summer.

Two of the three projects that represent nearly all of the Agriculture Department’s study of the parasite were defunded by Congress earlier this year, according to the department.

The third is slated to move from Maryland to Iowa this fall as part of a sweeping USDA reorganization. Even though that project still has money, every scientist working on the parasite has declined to relocate, according to three people familiar with the plans and documents shared with POLITICO, granted anonymity to discuss personnel issues.

The hollowing-out of all three projects, which was first reported by POLITICO, is expected to hinder vital food safety research at a time when Americans are increasingly worried that they can’t trust the food supply.

USDA is directing blame to Congress for zeroing out funds for two of the projects once housed at the agency’s Beltsville Agricultural Research Center just outside Washington. But the department’s broader relocation effort is also raising questions about the Trump administration’s work to overhaul vital research amid public health threats like cyclospora, salmonella and E. coli.

“We know so little, and I think that that’s been very frustrating to consumers,” said Kalmia Kniel, who studied with the BARC parasite scientists before becoming a professor researching cyclospora at the University of Delaware. Without BARC, “no one can work very fast. We don’t have the models, we don’t have these surrogates like we would want to have them, and we want to be able to do the research.”

More than 17,000 people have been sickened by cyclospora this summer, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The FDA is investigating multiple outbreaks of the parasite, including one that has sickened more than 11,000 people across 20 states. While scientific research couldn’t prevent the current outbreak, it could help investigators find the culprit faster next time — or prevent an outbreak in the first place.

The Trump administration has said BARC, a 6,500-acre complex where researchers study nutrition, animal health and food safety, is too expensive to keep open. USDA officials have also said the goal of the reorganization is to move the department’s employees closer to the people they serve and that research, like that in the labs that conduct cyclospora research, will be uninterrupted.

A USDA spokesperson blamed Congress for the funding cuts and said in a statement that “none of the research has been disrupted, and research will continue without disruption.”

“Congress did not appropriate funding for the two BARC research projects referenced in the FY2026 Agriculture Appropriations Act,” the USDA spokesperson added, noting that the USDA’s Agricultural Research Service “is working with research leaders to ensure an orderly transition of programs.”

Spokespeople for Republican and Democratic appropriators in the House and Senate who oversee the funding for the parasite research did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

“We’re basically not allowed to continue any research on that beyond trying to preserve the samples that we already have from previous outbreaks,” said a third USDA employee who worked on defunded cyclospora research that was done at BARC. “We see this as an enormous opportunity, this current outbreak, to have really a lot of samples that could help us understand these outbreaks better.”

Around the Agencies

CYCLOSPORA OUTBREAK UPDATE: The FDA reclassified a recall of Taylor Farms shredded iceberg lettuce imported from Mexico to Class I, the highest level of recall. The move signals the agency believes the affected product could cause serious health effects.

It doesn’t mean the recall has expanded, though, and FDA officials told reporters in a call Friday they are “confident” that the product associated with the recall is off store shelves. FDA investigators remain on site in Mexico in an effort to determine the source of the contamination at the processing plant that led to more than 11,000 lab-confirmed cases, according to the CDC.

The number of reported cyclospora cases related to this cluster continues to rise, especially since it can take weeks for illnesses to surface and for officials to confirm them.

The processing facility the FDA identified as the source of the outbreak is temporarily closed.

The FDA is continuing to investigate cyclospora clusters, but it has not identified any other sources of the parasite.

TRADE CORNER

TOOLS OF THE TRADE: Growers have faced higher tariffs on ag vehicles under the Trump administration’s metals duties, and industry representatives warn the administration is overlooking the tools amid its efforts to ease farmers’ tariff burden, Oliver writes in.

ATVs and their enclosed cousin, the utility terrain vehicle, are the workhorses of modern agriculture, with farmers and ranchers often using UTV cargo beds to haul tools, fertilizer and seeds across rugged terrain.

“They're not just luxury items,” Todd Cranney, the executive director of Save America’s Working Vehicles, told POLITICO, noting that the machines are ubiquitous on his family farm in southern Idaho.

The details: President Donald Trump sought to ease costs for farmers in a June proclamation offering temporary metals tariff reductions for a slate of ag machinery, including ATVs. But UTVs remain subject to the full 25 percent rate. Without an exclusions process like the one stood up in Trump’s first term, industries and companies are struggling to convey to the administration which products also have agricultural functions and warrant further relief.

The administration’s approach to offering tariff relief “is a little bit ad hoc,” said Cranney, whose coalition was launched shortly after the president’s June 1 proclamation reduced tariffs on some farm equipment.

“There isn't really a process at this point,” Cranney added, but he said he’d like to see that change. “We'd like to see an exemption when it comes to ATVs and UTVs, and we'd love to see a process for other issues as well.”

On the Hill

MA EXCLUSIVE: Senate Ag Committee ranking member Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) and 18 other senators raised concerns Sunday that the reorganization of the Foreign Agricultural Service will undermine its efficacy.

The senators sent a letter to Deputy Agriculture Secretary Stephen Vaden saying USDA’s relocation of FAS jobs to Missouri will hamper the international food aid programs the agency administers, such as the McGovern-Dole International Food for Education and Child Nutrition Program and Food for Progress.

“FAS has already experienced significant attrition, having lost over 25 percent of its employees since the end of 2024 and over 40 percent in the last decade,” the lawmakers wrote. “The USDA’s decision to require staff supporting foreign aid programs to move to Kansas City, Missouri, more than a third of the agency’s current staff, will only exacerbate these challenges.”

The senators, including Ag Committee members Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) asked Vaden to provide information about the reorganization, including a cost-benefit analysis and response to whether FAS programming timelines would be affected, by Sept. 14.

At the White House

MAKING MOO-VES: Trump said Friday that his administration will seek changes to allow farmers and ranchers to slaughter and process their own products in response to calls to loosen the grip of the big companies that dominate U.S. meat processing, as Grace reported.

“I am authorizing legal documents to be drawn in order to allow Farmers and Ranchers to be given the right to PROCESS THEIR OWN FOOD,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. “This should move quickly.”

The president’s announcement follows his proclamation earlier this week allowing an increase in beef imports over the next three months as part of a broader effort to bring down food prices ahead of the midterms. Trump also signaled his interest in addressing ranchers’ concerns about the so-called Big Four meat processors during an interview Wednesday with conservative commentator Glenn Beck.

The administration has already rolled out $60 million to bolster small meat processors and initiated an investigation into allegations that the Big Four meatpackers engaged in anti-competitive practices. The White House and USDA did not respond to questions about the timeline for the changes or the process for rolling them out.
